Today we will proceed to Lecture 8, with the theme being Fire Alarm System Design. This area represents one of the most frequent collaboration points between electrical engineering and other disciplines, while also constituting one of the largest portions of electrical-related content in international building codes.

Given its multidisciplinary coordination characteristics, we will dedicate specific time to explain fire alarm systems in detail.

This lecture is divided into two parts: Design & Installation and Verification. The design section will cover the following topics:

The necessity of fire alarm systems and their applicability in various construction projects, with specific regulations detailed in the North American Building Code.

A brief introduction to fire alarm systems, including system components.

Applicable codes and standards.

Types of fire alarm systems.

Fire alarm system design methodologies.

A brief introduction to fire alarm systems, including system components.

Applicable codes and standards.

Types of fire alarm systems.

Fire alarm system design methodologies.

As a critical component of electrical systems, the importance of fire alarm systems is self-evident.

The system is essential for detecting fires at an early stage and issuing alarms. All occupants of the building can evacuate promptly. Simultaneously, the system sends signals to the fire control center and activates corresponding fire protection equipment to prevent greater losses, especially casualties.

The primary function of this system is alarming rather than firefighting, as fire suppression is handled by the sprinkler system.

The primary function of this system is alarming rather than firefighting, as fire suppression is handled by the sprinkler system.

These devices are components of the fire alarm system, which are likely familiar to everyone, so we won’t elaborate further. The system primarily consists of the following parts: wiring, conduit installation, and the sequence and programming of the fire alarm system, which refers to the programming methods and control procedures. Design is an essential step. Additionally, the fire alarm system requires communication with the fire department, but in North America, not all projects have this requirement—it depends on the project’s scale and type. These details are clearly specified in building codes.

The controller of the fire alarm system, commonly referred to as the FACP (Fire Alarm Control Panel), is the core component responsible for processing various fire signals. These signals include fire alarm signals, the Super-Way Survey Signal for monitoring the valve status of the sprinkler system, and the Triple Signal for detecting valve closure in the fire hydrant system. As part of the fire protection system, the fire alarm system must be equipped with an emergency power supply. After the system’s design and construction are completed, testing, inspection, verification, operation, and maintenance are required. Compared to domestic standards, these requirements are more detailed abroad. Once the fire alarm system is completed, annual inspection and operational maintenance are still necessary each year.

The fire alarm system must be equipped with an emergency power supply as it is part of the fire protection system.

Emergency power supplies are divided into two categories: batteries and generators. For fire alarm systems, batteries are essential. Although AC power can be supplied by the mains or emergency power sources, the fire alarm system itself must be equipped with batteries.

The capacity of the battery must be determined according to building codes, with different requirements for different types of buildings. Specifically, the battery capacity design primarily considers its backup time. Typically, the battery must support the system’s operation for 24 hours in standby mode without a fire.

In the event of a fire, for high-rise buildings, the system must operate at full load (including alarm and linkage functions) for 2 hours continuously; for mid-rise buildings (e.g., 6 floors), it must operate for 1 hour; and for buildings with 4 floors or fewer, half an hour is sufficient. Therefore, the battery must have the corresponding capacity to meet the system’s requirements.

The fire alarm system is primarily composed of the following major categories.

The fire alarm system is primarily composed of the following major categories.

One category is called Initiating Devices. Initiating Devices include fire alarm buttons (domestically referred to as Pool Station), Heat Detectors, Smoke Detectors, Duct Smoke Detectors, as well as Combination Detectors that combine Heat and Smoke detection. Additionally, they include Flow Switches, Pressure Switches, and Control Valve Tamper Switches in sprinkler systems. Furthermore, VCO for elevators and Shutdown for air handling systems within the Initiating circuit also fall under Initiating Devices.

Another category is called Notification Devices, also known as Signaling Devices, which include Bells, Horns/Strobes, and Speakers, among others.

Another category is called Notification Devices, also known as Signaling Devices, which include Bells, Horns/Strobes, and Speakers, among others.

There is also a category of Auxiliary Devices, primarily referring to Monitoring Modules or Control Modules in fire alarm systems, which are essentially Relay-type devices. Additionally, this category includes End of Line Resistors and Zone Isolators, among others.

Taking Pool Station as an example, it is commonly referred to domestically as a manual alarm button and actually comes in two types: Code and Non-Code. The Code type is older and rarely used now, while the Non-Code type is more prevalent. Pool Stations are mainly divided into Single Action and Double Action types.

Single-Action refers to immediately sending a fire signal to the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) when pulled down.

Double-Action involves two steps: the first pull may generate a pre-alarm signal, which converts to a fire signal when fully pulled down.

Single-Action refers to immediately sending a fire signal to the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) when pulled down.

Double-Action involves two steps: the first pull may generate a pre-alarm signal, which converts to a fire signal when fully pulled down.

There are various types of fire detectors, among which heat detectors and smoke detectors are the most widely used.

Another type is the Duct Smoke Detector, primarily used in air conditioning supply ducts.

In industrial settings, there are also specialized detectors such as Fire Gas Detector and Flame Detector, the latter of which operates by detecting the optical signals of flames. Additionally, there are Smoke Detector and CO Detector, which are connected to fire alarm systems to form a Combined Detector.

Heat Detector comes in two types: one is fixed-temperature, while the other detects based on the rate of temperature rise.

There are two types of smoke detectors: ionization and photoelectric.

Heat detectors come in two types: one is fixed-temperature, while the other detects based on the rate of temperature rise.

There are two types of smoke detectors: ionization and photoelectric.

In terms of design, these aspects do not require excessive elaboration; it is only necessary to ensure their proper functionality. The LWX ionization smoke detector is typically installed at the supply and return air positions of air conditioning units. According to regulatory requirements, if the air conditioning system serves multiple fire compartments, floors, or units, a Hao Yuan photoelectric smoke detector must be installed in the supply air duct.

There are some differences between the standards in the United States and Canada.

There are some differences between the standards in the United States and Canada.

The U.S. standard requires determining installation requirements based on the air supply capacity of the air conditioning unit. If the airflow exceeds 2,000 CFM (cubic feet per minute), a smoke detector must be installed in the supply air duct; if it exceeds 15,000 CFM, an additional detector is required in the return air duct.

The Canadian standard, however, determines installation locations based on airflow velocity and duct cross-sectional dimensions. The purpose of these detectors is to trigger an alarm signal and shut down the air conditioning unit when smoke is detected in the supply or return air ducts.

Additionally, there are some specialized types of detectors. For example, duct-type smoke detectors (Pipe Smoke Detectors) are commonly used in large open spaces, particularly in archives. The detectors in this system are arranged along archive shelves and monitor smoke through probes, ultimately connecting the alarm signal to the building’s fire alarm system.

Another specialized detector is designed for high-rise, large-scale archives. This system installs transmitters and receivers at high levels, continuously emitting signals for monitoring. In the event of a fire, smoke interrupts signal transmission, triggering a fire alarm. This system can cover large spaces up to 50 meters in height.

Flame detectors are primarily used in locations such as oil fields, providing fire warnings by monitoring flame characteristics.

Flame detectors are primarily used in locations such as oil fields, providing fire warnings by monitoring flame characteristics.

Although the smoke does not decrease after ignition, flames will be produced. Therefore, ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) detectors are typically used for detection. This is not highly relevant to civil buildings and is only briefly introduced here. As for gas detectors, as mentioned earlier, they are primarily used to detect gases such as carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

Typically, they are available both as a standalone device and integrated with smoke detectors.

There are devices that combine smoke and temperature detection into one unit, as well as equipment that integrates smoke detection with carbon monoxide or carbon dioxide monitoring. Sprinkler systems might be less familiar to most people.

When working domestically, I didn’t know much about this aspect and didn’t pay enough attention to it. However, in reality, fire alarm systems are closely related to sprinkler systems. Below I will introduce several key devices in sprinkler systems:

First is the flow switch, which triggers a fire alarm signal when water flows through the sprinkler system pipes, indicating that the sprinkler heads have started discharging water. Next is the pressure switch, used to monitor water pressure in the pipes. When the pressure switch activates, it indicates that the sprinkler system has begun supplying water.

There is also the control valve temper switch. Sprinkler systems have control valves on each floor, which should normally remain open. If a valve is manually closed, that floor won’t receive sprinkler water supply in case of a fire. Therefore, when a valve is closed, this switch sends a supervisory signal to the fire alarm control panel to alert staff to reopen the valve promptly.

These devices are typically connected to the fire alarm system via monitoring modules. The aforementioned devices belong to initiating devices, while supervisory signals fall under notification signals.

Alternatively, signaling devices, including alarm bells, horns/strobes, and speakers.

In North America, speakers are commonly used in high-rise buildings because they can deliver voice notifications during a fire, whereas alarm bells or horns/strobes lack voice capabilities. Additionally, speakers typically operate in two-stage or horn/strobe mode. The specific standards and regulations for their application will be explained in detail later.

Regarding these products, for example in the US market, they must comply with UL and FM certification. FM certification is required by insurance companies as a prerequisite for insuring fire alarm systems. In Canada, fire alarm system products need to obtain ULC certification and meet relevant codes and standards.

Building codes specify whether various types of buildings require fire alarm systems, as well as details such as system type, connection requirements with fire control centers, detector placement, manual alarm station setup, and other related requirements. The codes also define technical requirements such as sound pressure levels for audible and visual alarm devices.

NEC and CEC primarily address wire selection and installation methods for fire alarm systems, falling under installation codes. Although focused on installation, these factors must also be thoroughly considered during design. In Canada, fire alarm system design mainly follows the ULC S524 standard, which covers both installation and design requirements. ULC S536 is the annual inspection standard, while ULC S537 specifies testing and verification requirements for new construction or renovation projects. Additionally, all components must meet other specific standards.

The primary standard in the US market is NFPA 72, which is equivalent to Canada’s ULC 524, 536, 537, etc. Other closely related standards include NFPA 13 and 20, with 20 being the standard for fire pumps.

NFPA 13 is the standard for sprinkler systems, which specifies the types of sprinkler systems to be used in different buildings. This part is primarily designed by Fire Protection Engineers in accordance with the standard.

Additionally, we need to understand local Building By-laws, as each city, state, or province has specific regulations for the design, installation, and acceptance of fire alarm systems. These regulations must be taken into account during the design, construction, installation, and commissioning of fire alarm systems.

Fire alarm systems can be classified in various ways, with the primary classification being single-stage systems and two-stage systems. A single-stage system immediately activates a fire alarm signal when triggered by manual pull stations, smoke detectors, heat detectors, water flow switches, pressure switches, or similar devices. In contrast, a two-stage system first issues an alert signal (volume signal) upon detecting such activation and only proceeds to a full fire alarm signal after a 3 to 5-minute confirmation period.

Building codes specify whether a single-stage or two-stage system should be used for particular structures. Two-stage systems are primarily employed in special facilities like hospitals, where frequent false alarms could cause significant disruption to immobile or treatment-dependent patients, such as those in ICUs or undergoing surgery.

Fire alarm systems can be categorized as coded or non-coded, with the latter typically being older systems. In terms of wiring, systems are divided into Class A and Class B circuits. Regarding zoning, a single fire compartment usually does not require further subdivision, though most projects still implement zoning configurations.

Currently, fire alarm systems predominantly rely on wired connections. However, with the rapid advancement of wireless technology, wireless alarm devices (e.g., detectors) are becoming increasingly common. While North America has not yet fully adopted wireless communication for these systems, it is anticipated that wireless technology will become the standard in the future.

The relevant content has been explained and will not be reiterated.

Now I will explain the difference between Class A and Class B. Class A typically adopts a closed-loop structure.

Class A typically adopts a closed-loop structure. This is a closed-loop system. When any part of the circuit is disconnected, both sides can still communicate back to the fire alarm control panel, ensuring high reliability without affecting system operation. In contrast, a Class B system behaves differently—if the circuit is interrupted midway, the subsequent sections will cease to function. This must be thoroughly considered during design.

In residential buildings where bedrooms are equipped with sprinkler systems, smoke detectors may not be mandatory according to the Canadian Electrical Code. However, each bedroom or unit must install alarm devices such as sirens or speakers, which typically require Class A systems; Class B systems are not permitted. In common areas like corridors, Class B systems are allowed.

The architectural discipline defines “fire zones” based on building codes. For example, elevator areas must meet a two-hour fire resistance requirement, and emergency stairwells are treated as independent fire compartments. Large spaces divided by firewalls are classified as separate fire compartments. This represents one classification approach to fire compartments in architecture.

Additionally, sprinkler systems have their own independent zoning. Meanwhile, fire alarm system zoning follows building codes and typically considers architectural fire compartments along with other factors. For instance, each flow switch or pressure switch in a sprinkler system constitutes a zone, as do smoke detectors. These zones are not visibly demarcated within buildings, making fire alarm system zoning generally more complex.

Non-zoned fire alarm systems consist of only one fire compartment or a single device, suitable for small buildings without fire compartment requirements. Finally, there are distinctions between addressable and conventional systems.

The primary distinction between addressable systems and conventional systems lies in the fact that the former possesses address encoding functionality, while the latter does not. Currently, most medium-to-large buildings commonly employ addressable fire alarm systems. However, conventional systems are still widely used in small-scale buildings across North America.

Conventional systems adopt a loop-based design, where each loop can only connect to a single fire compartment. In contrast, addressable systems allow a single loop to connect multiple fire compartments and precisely locate the fire’s origin through the address encoding of each smoke detector, heat detector, or water flow indicator.

Fire alarm system design must strictly comply with applicable building codes and standards. In British Columbia, Canada, the provincial building code is followed, while in the United States, the International Building Code or state-specific codes may apply. These codes specify whether a fire alarm system is required and define the system type—such as single-stage or two-stage—based on the building’s use and occupancy. Installation requirements for fire detectors are determined by building type and functional zones.

Code provisions include, but are not limited to:  
- Installation locations and types of alarm devices  
- Air handling unit shutdown linkage functionality  
- Interface requirements for elevators and fire doors

The code provisions cover multiple aspects, including but not limited to:  
- Installation locations and type requirements for alarm devices  
- Air handling unit shutdown linkage functionality  
- Interface requirements for elevators and fire doors  

During a fire incident, elevators must automatically return to designated floors (e.g., returning to a secondary floor if the main floor is affected); while fire door interfaces are used to control the open/close status of fire doors in large buildings or emergency stairwells.  

From an architectural perspective, the area is partitioned using firewalls or fire doors. Therefore, all doors on firewalls fall under the category of fire doors.  

In the event of a fire, these doors must remain closed to prevent the spread of smoke and flames to other areas. This design needs to work in coordination with the fire sprinkler system.

In the event of a fire, these doors must remain closed to prevent the spread of smoke and flames to other areas. This design needs to work in coordination with the fire sprinkler system.

The linkage mechanism is detailed in the relevant regulations and standards. The fire suppression system not only includes the sprinkler system, but also covers other types of fire suppression systems, such as dry and wet chemical systems. Special fire suppression systems are typically employed in data centers or high-risk areas. However, for ordinary buildings, sprinkler systems are generally used for fire suppression.

Sprinkler systems are mainly divided into two types: wet pipe systems and dry pipe systems. Wet pipe systems are always filled with water in the pipes, while dry pipe systems are used in areas without heating facilities, such as underground or outdoor parking lots. In these areas, winter temperatures may drop below freezing, which could cause water in the pipes to freeze. Therefore, dry pipe systems are filled with compressed air. When a fire occurs, the sprinkler heads open due to heat, releasing the air and allowing water to spray out.

The fire alarm system must be linked with equipment such as generators, and the zoning must be clearly defined in the design. The design should indicate the zoning of the fire alarm system so that manufacturers or contractors can number each detector according to the fire compartments. Additionally, the design must include the sequence of operation, which outlines the operational process in the event of a fire and serves as the basis for programming. All designs must comply with the relevant regulations and standards.

Regarding power supply requirements, details such as installation methods must be considered during the design phase, with specific reference to Clause 524 for implementation.

Regarding power supply requirements, details such as installation methods must be considered during the design phase, with specific reference to Clause 524 for implementation.

The requirements include battery capacity (Battery Size), as well as the layout specifications for fire alarm system equipment, such as the installation locations, spacing, ceiling height, and types of alarm bells and smoke detectors. The coverage range of smoke detectors and the decibel standards for alarm bells or strobe-horn devices are all governed by CAN/ULC-S524. In Canada, these technical requirements are defined by this standard, while in the U.S., NFPA 72 regulates the connection methods and coordination details between fire alarm systems and fire departments. Whether coordination is required is determined by the Building Code, with specific electrical technical details provided by CAN/ULC-S524 or NFPA 72.

Fire pump starting and monitoring requirements vary in North America, with fire alarm systems not directly starting fire pumps but instead monitoring their status signals, with slight differences in monitoring parameters between the U.S. and Canada. The U.S. requirements are more comprehensive.

Architectural floor plan including fire compartments and fire door locations.  
Building category determined by a Code Consultant or architect. Electrical engineers must design the system based on occupancy classifications (e.g., Occupancy A for theaters, Occupancy C for residential buildings) rather than arbitrarily placing equipment.  
Elevator room design requirements involving interface between the Elevator Controller and the fire alarm system. Electrical connections achieved via Control Mode Relays to ensure firefighter elevators are prioritized for recall to designated floors (e.g., Main Floor) during an alarm, while other elevators are taken out of service. Firefighters can control these elevators using a dedicated key.
HVAC system design drawings must indicate HVAC unit locations and airflow data (CFM) to design smoke detectors (Dark Smoke Detectors) and define the shutdown logic for HVAC systems during a fire.

All designs must strictly comply with relevant standards (e.g., CAN/ULC-S524, NFPA 72) and occupancy classification requirements.

In addition, the sprinkler system (Fire Protection) will mark the locations of flow switches, pressure switches, or temporal switches along with their controllers. The system diagrams and floor plans will guide the specific design. Finally, it is necessary to refer to the technical parameters of the fire alarm system provided by the manufacturer, such as the single-loop equipment capacity and signal transmission distance, as per the regulatory requirements.

In small to medium-sized projects, issues are generally minimal and can be mostly covered. However, for super high-rise or super large-scale buildings, relying solely on a single circuit running from start to finish is not feasible.

For example, some circuits allow a maximum of 128 connected devices, or have cable length limits of 3,000 feet—these factors must be considered.

Regarding whether an L-Handler requires installation of a dark smoke detector, the NIP-90A standard mentioned earlier specifies: when the CFM value exceeds 2,000, detectors must be installed in both supply and return air ducts.

When the CFM value exceeds 2,000, detectors must be installed in both supply and return air ducts.

Building codes have clear requirements for the installation location of Fire Alarm Control Panels (FACP). Unlike the domestic practice of establishing large fire control centers with dedicated personnel, local regulations adopt a centralized monitoring approach. For large-scale projects, the fire alarm system controller must establish communication links with third-party monitoring companies or centers certified under ULC561. These certified institutions provide 24/7 monitoring services—when the system triggers an alarm signal, the monitoring center immediately verifies the alert and notifies the fire department for dispatch.

Upon arrival at the scene, firefighters will first proceed to either the Fire Alarm Control Panel (standard equipment in large/medium-sized buildings, typically located in electrical rooms) or the Annunciator at the main entrance. These two interconnected devices share real-time fire zone localization data via communication lines, displaying specific incident locations such as pump rooms on the 5th floor, smoke detectors on the 7th floor, or flow switches on the 10th floor.

This design ensures rapid situational awareness and effective command decisions by firefighters. The synchronized operation between annunciators and main control panels provides critical technical support for initial fire response and false alarm identification.

For small and medium-sized buildings, the Fire Alarm Control Panel (FACP) and Annunciator can be combined into a single unit. This control panel must be installed in a conspicuous location, such as the main entrance, and within a fire-rated wall area. In small buildings with limited fire-rated wall zones, it may be placed directly at the main entrance.

The Fire Alarm Power Supply has been discussed earlier. In North America, medium-sized and larger buildings typically require a dedicated Code Consultants Report. This report focuses on Building Code consulting services, covering the overall building code requirements and referencing the Electrical Code. Code consultants are highly familiar with building codes but may lack detailed knowledge of Electrical Code implementation. They provide comprehensive code analysis and issue formal reports.

Fire Alarm System Design often references this report. While industry roles are specialized, I personally consult this report during design while maintaining deep familiarity with the codes. In practice, independent design is feasible even without the report. However, inexperienced designers may struggle with fire alarm system design.

Regarding design drawing specifications, all essential elements of fire alarm system design must be included.

First, it is necessary to prepare the Layout (i.e., the floor plan) to clarify the placement of smoke detectors, heat detectors, and the installation location of the Fire Alarm Panel.

Next is the Riser Diagram (i.e., the system diagram). Additionally, a Zone Schedule must be provided, detailing the zoning of the fire alarm system, which typically includes hundreds of zones.

Next is the Riser Diagram (i.e., the system diagram). Additionally, a Zone Schedule must be provided, detailing the zoning of the fire alarm system, which typically includes hundreds of zones.

The Fire Alarm Sequence of Operation specifies the specific measures to be taken in the event of a fire. The fire alarm system design specifications and related installation details are also necessary, but these are usually handled by experienced contractors and do not require overly complex design.

The battery capacity (Sizing of battery) is generally determined by the manufacturer based on relevant standards. The design documents only need to note that the electrical contractor and fire alarm manufacturer should determine the battery capacity according to the standards. The floor plan must indicate the installation locations of alarm devices.

The positions of detectors and Pool Station do not need to be connected, only their locations need to be marked. The Riser Diagram is used to display floor distribution, equipment configuration, and their connection methods.

Of course, this does not mean connecting all devices but rather a representative demonstration. For example, if there are 100 devices in the system, it is impossible to depict all of them in a single circuit, hence the use of schematic diagrams.

Here, the Fire Alarm Control Panel is displayed, connected to different alarm circuits, namely the Initiating Circuit or Signaling Circuit. Typically, Initiating Circuits—such as those for Pull Stations or Smoke Detectors—require Class A wiring, while Signaling Circuits—such as those for Notification Appliances (including Horns, Bells, Speakers, etc.)—may use Class B wiring, though specific regulatory requirements must be followed.

One approach is to directly shut down the corresponding air handling unit (AHU) via hardwired interlock when a duct smoke detector detects a fire signal, but this method is not recommended.

Another approach is for the fire alarm system to send a signal to the building automation system (BAS) when a fire occurs in the entire building, which then shuts down the AHU. This method is also not recommended because the more links in the chain, the lower the reliability.

In practice, a third method is more commonly used and reliable: the fire alarm system directly controls the AHU’s controller to shut it down.

Additionally, the monitoring function of the sprinkler system is not directly activated by the fire alarm system but is triggered by a pressure switch, though the fire alarm system needs to monitor its signal.

In the event of a fire, elevators are prohibited from use, and evacuation must be conducted via stairwells. Simultaneous smoke exhaust and positive pressure ventilation must be implemented in the stairwells. The fatality rate due to smoke inhalation in fires far exceeds that from direct burns. The positive pressure ventilation system supplies fresh air to the stairwells, ensuring unobstructed breathing for evacuees, while the smoke exhaust system expels smoke outdoors. Both systems must be activated simultaneously during a fire.

Under normal conditions, the system is equipped with fire dampers or smoke dampers. Taking stairwells as an example, the positive pressure fans and smoke exhaust fans are typically located outdoors and connected via ducts. When ducts pass through firewalls, fire dampers must be installed. These valves include electrically controlled types and gravity-operated automatic-closing types. During a fire, the fire damper control system must open them; otherwise, airflow will be obstructed.

All elevators shall return to the main floor. In case of a fire on the main floor, they shall return to the second floor; if a fire occurs on the second floor, they shall proceed to the third floor. Fire-rated doors located on firewalls must be closed to isolate the burning and non-burning fire compartments.

During evacuation, certain fire doors must remain operational for passage. For instance, when integrated with access control systems or security systems, some doors are equipped with magnetic locks or electrical strikes. Magnetic locks automatically release upon power loss, allowing the door to open, while remaining locked when powered. During a fire, power to such doors must be cut to ensure unobstructed evacuation routes.

Furthermore, these designs require coordination with architectural disciplines to guarantee unimpeded fire escape routes. Other related measures include elevator recall, fire door closure, etc. In the North American market, major manufacturers include Simplex and Notifier.

I have a question to ask: In your lecture, you mentioned that the air conditioning system needs to be interconnected with the fire alarm system, and detectors also need to be installed in the air conditioning ducts.

Is this practice common in North America?

In domestic design practices, it appears this approach is not commonly adopted for air conditioning systems. Could you please provide further detailed clarification?

Of course, this is not a matter of commonality. In domestic design practices, we tend to focus on prevalence, but here, the code mandates strict compliance—there is no room for negotiation. For instance, some projects may complete the installation of fire alarm systems within a month or two, yet many details remain superficially addressed. In contrast, international projects allocate at least five times the time and cost of domestic ones, resulting in far more meticulous execution. If code-required measures are neglected, accountability will be enforced.

Electrical engineers often lack sufficient cross-disciplinary knowledge. Electrical engineering serves other disciplines, so a deep understanding of related fields is essential. For example, in designing architectural fire compartments, a thorough grasp of adjacent disciplines and clear coordination mechanisms are necessary.

Regarding concealed smoke detectors and HVAC unit shutdowns, an HVAC system functions as a circulatory network. Smoke detectors are installed in supply or return air ducts for two primary reasons:  
1. Building air circulates through HVAC units. If smoke is present, it spreads via airflow. Duct-mounted detectors enable early smoke detection.  
2. This protects HVAC units from fire damage. Units contain electric heaters and motors; detectors in ducts trigger fire protection signals upon smoke detection.

HVAC units must shut down during a fire because continued operation would fuel combustion. For example, if an HVAC unit supplies multiple floors and one floor catches fire, ongoing airflow would deliver fresh oxygen, accelerating fire spread. Immediate shutdown is imperative. As electrical engineers, we must develop expertise in adjacent fields—including building automation systems—through accumulated experience. Since HVAC units exacerbate fires, their immediate deactivation is non-negotiable.

There are differences in power supply management during fires between domestic and international practices. The domestic approach is to cut off non-emergency power supplies during a fire, retaining only firefighting power sources. In contrast, international standards prioritize ensuring safe evacuation. For example, relying solely on emergency lighting during a fire may result in insufficient illumination, hindering evacuation. Thus, international standards permit other lighting systems to remain operational to facilitate rapid evacuation. Equipment damage is not the primary concern during a fire; rescue and fire suppression take precedence.

For air conditioning systems, they must be shut down if they risk exacerbating the fire. Based on this principle, fire detectors should be installed in supply and return air ducts, and the air conditioning power must be cut off during a fire. However, exceptions exist: if the air conditioning serves only a single fire compartment, it need not be shut down as it does not affect other areas; if it provides circulating air supply to multiple fire compartments, it must be turned off to prevent the spread of flames and smoke to other compartments. This logic clearly reflects the core philosophy behind standard formulation.

Yes, the concept of non-emergency forced power cutoff does not exist in North America.

The concept of debugging in the Chinese context generally refers to ensuring the system can operate normally. However, in North America, debugging not only requires the system to pass tests but also involves completing comprehensive documentation. Additionally, it must comply with relevant application specifications and standards.

Regarding the debugging of fire alarm systems, the scope of work includes specific technical document submission requirements and necessary input conditions. When conducting tests, the instruments and equipment used, as well as the testing procedures, must be clearly defined. Furthermore, the installation must adhere to the latest regulatory requirements.

After installation is completed, the fire alarm system needs to be programmed. Programming is carried out based on fire compartments and preset sequences, typically performed by manufacturer technicians, such as Level 35 technicians from companies like Siemens, Honeywell, and Johnson Controls, who complete the programming and verification tasks.

Additionally, as-built drawings must be submitted after installation. Before ordering materials during the initial installation phase, shop drawings and operation & maintenance manuals (O&M package) need to be prepared.
